source.authors: Gaudet K, Faraone N, Hillier NK
source.title: Investigating chemoreception and behavioural responses of Tetranychus urticae (Trombidiformes: Tetranychidae) to organic acids, aldehydes and essential oil components

value: repelled by butyric acid at 100 ng/mL (p < 0.001) and not at 10 ng/mL (p = 0.1)
method: two-choice behavioural assay: one bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) leaf dipped halfway in the compound in 0.1% v/v Tween-80, the other half solvent only, split by a 5 mm filter-paper strip along the primary vein; one mite per trial watched for 20 min
conditions: doses 10 and 100 ng/mL; n = 50 (Figure 6 legend, as returned by the fetch summary); female mites (sex stated for the solvent controls); the Tween-80 carrier was itself not repellent; non-responders excluded; binomial test against 50%; responder count per dose not given in text
quote: Tetranychus urticae was repelled by butyric acid at 100 ng/mL (p < 0.001), but not at 10 ng/mL (p = 0.1).
note: Licence: CC BY (page statement 'open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)'; Crossref lists CC BY 4.0). Read on the Frontiers PDF through WebFetch, the summariser returning the quoted sentence intact in two fetches. Name accepted in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Dose-dependent: the sentence is a repellency result at the higher dose only. Exceptions in the same section, read from the fetch summary and not as quoted sentences: eucalyptol was not significantly repelled at either dose, linalool and thymol were repelled at 100 but not 10 ng/mL, and no compound was reported attractive. Stimulus is a leaf-surface dose in ng/mL, not an airborne concentration.

source.authors: Gaudet K, Faraone N, Hillier NK
source.title: Investigating chemoreception and behavioural responses of Tetranychus urticae (Trombidiformes: Tetranychidae) to organic acids, aldehydes and essential oil components

value: mean peak electrotarsogram amplitude 0.132 mV ± 0.0223 to butyric acid
method: gas chromatography-linked electrotarsal detection (GC-ETD): adult female mounted dorsally on a Syntech fork electrode, foretarsi in electrode gel under the recording electrode; stimulus is GC effluent from a 1 µL splitless injection of a carboxylic-acid master mix at 1 mg/mL in hexane (DB-5 column, helium 1.2 mL/min)
conditions: n = 7 (Figure 5A); ± not defined; no solvent baseline or test against one reported for GC-ETD amplitudes. Separately, in the puff ETG screen (0.3 s puffs, 10 ng to 10 mg, hexane-subtracted, n = 20) butyric acid at 10000 ng gave 0.923 ± 1.011 mV, different from hexane (Tukey p < 0.001, Table 1), and amplitudes differed among compounds (F7,20 = 5.76, p < 0.001)
where: Results, Gas chromatography-linked electrotarsal detection; Figure 5A
quote: Butyric acid, a 4-carbon carboxylic acid, had a mean peak amplitude of 0.132 mV ± 0.0223.
note: Licence: CC BY (page statement 'open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)'; Crossref lists CC BY 4.0). Read on the Frontiers PDF through WebFetch, the summariser returning the quoted sentence intact in two fetches. Name accepted in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Tarsal (foreleg) response, not an antennal EAG: mites have no antennae. Butyric acid also repelled mites in the behavioural assay at 100 ng/mL (separate record).

source.authors: Gaudet K, Faraone N, Hillier NK
source.title: Investigating chemoreception and behavioural responses of Tetranychus urticae (Trombidiformes: Tetranychidae) to organic acids, aldehydes and essential oil components

value: mean peak electrotarsogram amplitude 0.0973 mV ± 0.0197 to eucalyptol
method: gas chromatography-linked electrotarsal detection (GC-ETD): as for butyric acid, but the stimulus is GC effluent from a 1 µL splitless injection of an essential-oil master mix (linalool, thymol, eucalyptol) at 100 ng/mL per compound in hexane
conditions: n = 6 (Figure 5C); ± not defined; master mix 10 000 times more dilute than the carboxylic-acid mix, so not comparable with the butyric-acid amplitude; eucalyptol was not in the puff ETG screen and no comparison with hexane is reported for it
where: Results, Gas chromatography-linked electrotarsal detection; Figure 5C
quote: Eucalyptol had a mean peak amplitude of 0.0973 mV ± 0.0197.
note: Licence: CC BY (page statement 'open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)'; Crossref lists CC BY 4.0). Read on the Frontiers PDF through WebFetch, the summariser returning the quoted sentence intact in two fetches. Name accepted in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Contrary behavioural result: in the two-choice assay eucalyptol was not significantly repelled at either 10 or 100 ng/mL (fetch summary), the GC-ETD peak has no reported baseline test, so the paper does not show a tarsal response distinguishable from solvent; behaviourally eucalyptol was not repelled at 10 or 100 ng/mL (p = 0.4; p = 0.2).

source.authors: Piou V, Vilarem C, Blanchard S, Armengaud C, Heeb P, Vétillard A
source.title: Varroa destructor relies on physical cues to feed in artificial conditions

value: females with the foreleg sensory pit (main olfactory organ) blocked still found the feeding site and fed
method: artificial feeding chambers (PBS under Parafilm); sensory pit on the forelegs covered with nail polish, controls marked with nail polish on the dorsal scutum
conditions: 86.4% of sense-deprived females fed (n = 44) against 81.1% of nail-polish controls (n = 37), no significant difference (percentages seen as quoted fragments, n from the fetch summary); the sense was blocked, not ablated, and the authors describe the pit as the main olfactory organ in the Discussion; two mites per chamber, analysed per mite; feeding scored by blue dye in the gut at 24 h; only the foreleg sensory pit was covered
quote: The mites were still able to detect the feeding site when deprived of the sensory pit.
note: Licence: CC BY 4.0 (page statement and Crossref). Read on the journal PDF through WebFetch. Name: NZOR lists Varroa destructor Anderson & Trueman, 2000 as the preferred, in-use name (NZOR prints the family as 'Varoidae', a typo for Varroidae, Plazi lists Varroidae Delfinado & Baker 1974); not in gbif-names.tsv and no GBIF page reached. Null result: blocking the sensory pit did not reduce feeding in this artificial set-up, so it does not show the pit is unused in the hive. Discussion and Results figures for PBS versus Parafilm feeding appear swapped in the fetch summary (93%/96%); not carried here.

source.authors: Piou V, Vilarem C, Blanchard S, Armengaud C, Heeb P, Vétillard A
source.title: Varroa destructor relies on physical cues to feed in artificial conditions

value: in artificial feeding chambers without honey bee odour, females were still able to feed guided only by physical cues
method: artificial feeding designs with PBS under Parafilm: flat membrane (disc) against a rounded bubble; behaviour scored in test arenas
conditions: feeding in chambers not rubbed with a bee pupa 100% (N = 32) against 92.9% in rubbed chambers (N = 140), no difference across four odour treatments (bias-reduced GLM, df = 3, χ² = 4.25, p = 0.24); in arenas (blue PBS under Parafilm, no bee odour) time on a 3D bubble 55.2 ± 6.1% against 4.9 ± 1.3% of 10 min on a flat disc (N = 32, p < 0.001); the authors say detection 'seems to be shape-related'; Parafilm may pass small volatiles
quote: We found that V. destructor is still able to feed only guided by physical cues.
note: Licence: CC BY 4.0 (page statement and Crossref). Read on the journal PDF through WebFetch. Name: NZOR lists Varroa destructor Anderson & Trueman, 2000 as the preferred, in-use name (NZOR prints the family as 'Varoidae', a typo for Varroidae, Plazi lists Varroidae Delfinado & Baker 1974); not in gbif-names.tsv and no GBIF page reached. The abstract goes on to say detection of the food source seems shape-related because a 3D membrane triggers arrestment and exploration (cut sentence). Parafilm may pass small volatiles, which the authors note, so chemical cues are not fully excluded.

value: chose the darkest grey target (G45) over the five lighter greys and the background grey; the brightest grey (G225) was second and the mid grey G135 least attractive
method: laboratory multiple-choice arena (glass Petri dish with coloured wall targets); each psyllid tested once, individually, for up to 30 min; Experiment 3 offered shades of grey
conditions: Experiment 3: six spectrally flat greys (G45 to G225, 4 × 4 cm) on a G166 background (35% reflecting), reflectance measured 300 to 800 nm (Figure 2B), intensity contrast computed; n = 113, G²(113, 6) = 71.4, p < 0.001; G45 against G225 p < 0.05, against the others p < 0.001 (sequential Bonferroni); illumination about 5180 lux, arena rotated between trials; Glycaspis brimblecombei showed no significant attraction to a specific grey

source.authors: Farnier K, Dyer AG, Steinbauer MJ
source.title: Related but not alike: not all Hemiptera are attracted to yellow

quote: Anoeconeossa bundoorensis preferred the darkest target (G45) to the others.
note: Licence: CC BY (notice printed on the Frontiers PDF read through WebFetch). Crossref, queried for author order and volume, returned no licence and no article number; the PDF header gives Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution volume 2, article 67, October 2014. Name: the repo's gbif-names.tsv maps the spelling 'Anoeconesossa bundoorensis' (used in the earlier main row (canon-4:72)) to the accepted Anoeconeossa bundoorensis; family, order and class follow the the earlier main row (canon-4:72). The summariser also returned that the Results sentence on grey shades for G. brimblecombei begins 'However' and does not name the species, so no record is filed for it. Not a measured spectral sensitivity: a target-choice preference the greys are spectrally flat and differ in intensity; the ranking (darkest first, brightest second) fits contrast against the background as well as darkness.
